**Research note: PostgreSQL identifier length, column count, and connection defaults**

Three limits come up when sizing a new schema and its pool. All three are stated in the current PostgreSQL manual, and I read the relevant pages rather than relying on memory.

**Identifier length.** PostgreSQL uses no more than NAMEDATALEN minus one bytes of any identifier. NAMEDATALEN is a compile-time constant that defaults to 64, so the default maximum identifier length is 63 bytes (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). The limits appendix lists the same figure, 63 bytes, and notes it can only be raised by recompiling the server (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). Two practical points follow. Longer names are not rejected but silently truncated with a notice, which can cause two long names to collide. The limit is in bytes, not characters, so non-ASCII identifiers run out of room sooner.

**Columns per table.** The limits appendix gives an upper limit of 1,600 columns per table. The same row adds that the real ceiling is further limited by the tuple having to fit on a single page, so wide column types reduce the usable number well below 1,600 (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). Dropped columns still count toward the limit until the table is rewritten, so a table that is churned through many migrations can hit it earlier than its visible column count suggests.

**Default max_connections.** The connection settings documentation states that the default is typically 100 connections, but it may be lower if kernel settings at initdb time cannot support it. The parameter can only be changed at server start, and PostgreSQL allocates shared memory and other resources in proportion to it, so raising it is not free (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). On a standby, the value must be at least as high as on the primary or queries will be refused.

**Recommendation.** Keep all identifiers comfortably under 63 bytes with a naming convention enforced in migrations, and keep tables far narrower than the 1,600 limit by normalising rather than adding columns. Size the application pool against the server's actual max_connections value, leaving headroom below 100 for superuser and maintenance sessions, and prefer a small pool per instance with a pooler like PgBouncer over raising max_connections.
